tagline.text: A protected island south of Guimaras with preserved mangroves, coral and sandbars

location.label: Location
location.text: Taklong Island, off Nueva Valencia in southern Guimaras

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–2,000 (per person, sharing a chartered boat, including lunch)

children.text: Taklong Island is a protected island off Nueva Valencia in southern Guimaras that became a national marine reserve in 1990. Mangrove forest, coral, seagrass beds and sandbars remain in good condition, and you can see them easily on a boat tour with snorkeling.

Taklong Island lies off Nueva Valencia at the southern end of Guimaras, facing Panay Gulf. According to Wikipedia, President Corazon Aquino declared it a national marine reserve on February 8, 1990, and in 2025 Republic Act No. 12225 converted it into the Taklong and Tandog Group of Islands Natural Park, with Taklong as its main island. If the island of Guimaras is a destination of mangoes, a monastery and beaches, this island is about marine conservation, so even within Guimaras you see a completely different landscape.

The reserve brings together mangrove forest, seagrass beds and coral reef. Presidential Proclamation No. 525 of 1990 gives the size of the reserve as about 1,143 hectares (1,143.45 ha). According to an introduction by the Partnerships in Environmental Management for the Seas of East Asia (PEMSEA), 66 bird species, 6 mammal species and at least 16 reptile species live here, and 26 mangrove species, 9 seagrass species and 77 seaweed species have been recorded. Long-tailed macaques, giant island fruit bats and Philippine ducks are said to be seen often, so approaching the coastal forest by boat is also rewarding. The reserve is designated a protected landscape and seascape, commercial and destructive fishing are banned, and only handline fishing is allowed. As a result it works as a breeding ground where fish spawn and grow, and in 2017 it is reported to have won first place as Most Outstanding NIPAS marine protected area at the Para el Mar Awards.

The island has a marine station run by the University of the Philippines Visayas (UPV). According to Wikipedia, the station was built in 1977 and renovated in 1987 and 2008, on a parcel of about 1.64 hectares donated in 1964. When the reserve was proclaimed in 1990, only one family lived on the island, which shows how little touched it still is. At the back of the island, a dock runs through the mangroves and is known as the one used when the sea is rough. Facilities on the island run off-grid on solar power and rainwater, and a watchtower, an information center, a floating cottage, a gazebo and a conference room are said to be available. Visitor numbers are limited to the island's carrying capacity under the development plan of the Protected Area Management Board.

When the tanker Solar 1 sank in 2006 and oil spread, Taklong's mangrove forest was also badly hit, and Wikipedia says about 90 percent of the mangroves were coated with oil sludge. Rehabilitation followed: La Paz Fisherfolk Resources and Mangrove Management Inc. (Lafarma) has replanted mangroves under the National Greening Program since 2011 and reports keeping a survival rate of at least 85 percent. Knowing this story makes the green forest and shallow sea feel much more precious. Former illegal fishers now take part in patrols and persuade other fishers to follow the rules. Please remember that this reserve is protected by the local community itself when you visit.

blocks.title: Mangrove forest and the back dock

children.text: The dock through the mangroves at the back of the island is the one used when the sea is rough. The forest serves as a nursery and habitat for fish and shrimp, and you can see how it has been restored since the 2006 oil spill.
According to travel guides, boats anchor at designated points for snorkeling. You can see colorful coral reefs and tropical fish up close. Ask your boatman first which points are open.
The island is connected to neighboring islands by two sandbars, one of which is the Banago sandbar. Some sandbars are free, while others reportedly charge an entrance fee.

The island is described as having an eco-trail through the forest and several caves. Check with the reserve management office before your visit about which sections are open and whether guides are provided.
Built in 1977, the station is a site for marine ecology research. A limited number of people may stay overnight with permission from the management authority and UPV, so inquire in advance if needed.
Waterbirds such as the Philippine duck, giant island fruit bats and long-tailed macaques are said to be seen often. Watch quietly and do not feed them.
Tours usually return across the Guimaras Strait around sunset. Watching fishing boats and seabirds pass in the evening light is the highlight.

blocks.title: A reserve protected by the community

children.text: The reserve is managed jointly by the environment department, provincial and municipal governments, barangays and people's organizations, and groups such as Lafarma provide livelihood support and training. Respect the explanations and rules of local guides.

items.title: Half-day boat tour
items.subtitle: Seeing Taklong Island from Iloilo City

children.text: Take a boat from Ortiz Wharf in Iloilo City across to Jordan (about 15 minutes).
Check island-hopping boats and fares at the Jordan tourism office, then head to a pier on the Nueva Valencia side.
Hire a boat at a pier such as Dungcaan and set off for Taklong Island (about 20–30 minutes).
Look around the island's shore and mangroves, and snorkel at designated points.
Eat a packed lunch on a sandbar or beach.
Stop by the sandbar of a neighboring island (such as Gamay Island) and take photos.
Cross the strait back to the pier and take a boat to Iloilo.
For a private tour, the cost per person rises when there are few people. Gather a group and share the boat.
Visit the Trappist Monastery in Jordan and buy mango products.
Have lunch near Alubihod Beach and check in.
See Guisi Lighthouse and Guisi Beach and watch the sunset.
Take an island-hopping boat on a tour around Taklong and neighboring islands.
Return to Jordan Wharf and cross to Iloilo.
Direct flights run from Manila to Iloilo International Airport (ILO). Guimaras has no airport, so you must go through Iloilo.
The airport is away from the city, so take a shuttle van or taxi toward Ortiz Wharf in the city.

Other piers closer to the reserve are said to have steep access roads. Follow the pier your boatman recommends.
Island-hopping tours can be combined with an overland Guimaras course or booked as a private tour.
It is said to be about 13 km from Jordan to the center of Nueva Valencia. Ask the tourism office about pier locations and transfer fares.
Taklong is an outdoor trip around the sea and islands, so the dry season, when it is clear and the sea is calm, is best. When it is clear, the water color is vivid and snorkeling visibility is wider.
In the rainy season or typhoon season, waves in the strait can get high and boats may not go out. Note also that the dock at the back in the mangroves is the one used when the sea is rough.

There is no general lodging in the reserve itself. One source says a limited number of people may stay at the UPV marine station with permission from the management authority and the university, but it is not for ordinary tourists, so inquire in advance. Most visitors stay at Alubihod Beach in Nueva Valencia or in the town of Jordan. One guide says beach cottages usually start from
, so check before booking.

There are almost no shops on the island. One traveler wrote that nearby stores are few and sell mostly simple snacks. Bring a packed lunch, water and extra snacks. Because this is a mangrove protected area, take all your trash back after eating. If the timing works, you could also aim for the mango festival in April.
One guide says the reserve manages visitors so that there are no more than 30 at a time, so groups should inquire with the management in advance.
Bring cash. Boat fares and entrance fees are paid in cash on site.
Some areas charge entrance and boat parking fees separately. Ask your boatman for the total first.
Check first whether snorkeling gear is included in the tour.
Bring lunch, water, sunscreen and a hat. There is little shade and few shops on the island.
Do not step on or break mangroves and coral, and take all your trash with you.
Small bills, a waterproof bag and aqua shoes are useful.
One guide says visits of more than 30 people at a time need approval from the environment department and the reserve managers, so groups must inquire in advance.
Environmental protection comes first in the reserve, so visitor numbers and activities may be limited. Check the latest guidance from the reserve management for individual access rules.
Commercial and destructive fishing is banned and only handline fishing is allowed. Do not use nets or spears.
Boat fares and entrance fees come from sources dated 2017–2022 and may have changed. Agree on the price with your boatman before departure.
Crossing the strait is dangerous when the sea is rough, so judge locally whether it is safe to sail.
Do not touch coral or mangroves, and do not feed wildlife.
This is a remote island, so bring personal medication and first-aid supplies.
There are reports that reserve staff have been threatened by illegal fishers. If you see a violation, do not intervene yourself but report it to the management office.
